I want the app under test to hit my own listener instead of mobile-api.shopwave.io, without editing its config or /etc/hosts.

Hook the resolution itself — burpwn's shim sees the query before it goes upstream:

```
burpwn --json hook add pin-api \
  --phase dns-query \
  --host mobile-api.shopwave.io \
  --action set-answer --answer 127.0.0.1
```

```json
{"data": {"hook_id": 2, "name": "pin-api"}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

The sandboxed workload now resolves that name to your address, with no file to edit and nothing left behind on the host — the hook is scoped to the session.

Read the scope flags carefully here, because they are reused rather than renamed: on `dns-query`, **`--host` is the queried NAME** (a case-insensitive substring, so `--host shopwave.io` would catch every subdomain), and `--path` is the record type written as `/A`, `/AAAA` or `/TXT`.

Only `A` and `AAAA` queries are answered — give it an IPv4 or IPv6 address and it replies with that record. Anything else (`TXT`, `MX`, `SRV`) still goes upstream even if the hook matches, so this steers connections, it does not forge a whole zone.

To make a name simply fail to resolve instead — cutting an analytics or update endpoint out of the run — drop the query:

```
burpwn --json hook add no-telemetry --phase dns --host telemetry --action drop
```

```json
{"data": {"hook_id": 3, "name": "no-telemetry"}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

`dns` is accepted as an alias for `dns-query`. `drop` is the one action that means the same thing on every phase.

I set up a match/replace rule to add an `X-CSRF-Token` header to my requests and it does nothing. The rule looks right.

The rule is right; it just cannot do that job. **match/replace rewrites what is already in the message** — it matches an existing header and substitutes it. If the request never carried `X-CSRF-Token`, there is nothing for the pattern to match, so the rule correctly does nothing.

Synthesising a header that is absent is a hook's `add-header` action:

```
burpwn --json hook add force-csrf --action add-header --header "X-CSRF-Token: probe-value" --host shop.northwind.example
```

```json
{"data": {"hook_id": 1, "name": "force-csrf"}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

That's the whole distinction, and it's the one that decides which feature to reach for:

Each WebSocket message needs a fresh HMAC. Can I put an exec hook on ws-c2s to sign them?

No — burpwn refuses that pairing outright rather than accepting it and disappointing you on the wire:

```
burpwn --json hook add sign-frames --phase ws-c2s --action exec \
  --cmd './sign.sh' --extract '^(.*)$' --inject-header 'X-Sig: {}'
```

```json
{"data": null, "error": "[BW-INPUT-001] the exec action does not apply to a ws-c2s hook \u2014 an exec hook runs a command in a sandbox, and a ws-c2s hook fires on every message the socket carries \u2014 one sandbox each would cost more than the traffic it watches. Put the exec hook on pre-request: a socket inherits what its upgrade request carried", "ok": false}
```

The reason is cost, not meaning. An `exec` hook runs its command **in the sandbox**, and one command is one sandbox; a busy socket carries thousands of messages, so signing each one would serialize the proxy behind a process spawn per frame.

The error also tells you the way round, and it is a real one: put the `exec` hook on `--phase pre-request` scoped to the **upgrade request**. A socket inherits what its upgrade carried, so a token or signature injected there applies for the life of the connection.

If the per-message value genuinely has to change per message, that is not a hook job — capture the socket and drive it yourself from a script under `burpwn exec`.

The same refusal covers `dns-query`, for the same reason (one sandbox per name resolved). What IS allowed on these phases is only what needs no process: `drop` everywhere, `replace-payload` on `ws-*`, `set-answer` on `dns-query`.

Add an X-CSRF-Token header to my requests to shop.northwind.example — the requests don't currently have one. I tried match_replace_add and nothing happened.
match_replace_add cannot do this: it substitutes into what the message already contains. Synthesising an absent header is a hook's add-header action.

messages.name: hook_add

messages.content: That's why the rule did nothing: **match/replace rewrites an existing header**, so with no `X-CSRF-Token` in the request there was nothing for it to match. A hook's `add-header` action **creates** the header. Hook 1 is now live and will synthesise `X-CSRF-Token: probe-value` on every request to that host. Rule of thumb: `match_replace_add` when it is already there and you want it changed, `hook_add add-header` when it is not there and you want it to exist, `set-header` when you want either.

* **what burpwn stored** — dropped outright: the auth profiles' login commands, the recorded `burpwn exec` command lines, and the `replacement` field of your match/replace rules.
* **what burpwn captured** — masked in the recorded requests and responses: `Authorization`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `Cookie` and `Set-Cookie` headers, plus `password`/`token`/`api_key`-style parameters.

```
  --extract '"access_token":"([^"]+)"' \
  --inject-header 'Authorization: Bearer {}' \
```

```json
{"data": null, "error": "[BW-INPUT-009] hook 1 is a ws-c2s hook: `hook test` replays a hook against a captured HTTP request or response, and neither exists for that phase. Watch it on live traffic instead (`req list --protocol ws` / `--protocol dns`)", "ok": false}
```

`hook test` works by replaying a hook against a **captured HTTP message** and diffing before/after. A WebSocket message is not one — the frames live in their own table — and a DNS query is a name, not a request. The order book on app.fintrack.dev runs over a WebSocket, so my match/replace rules never fire on it. Can I tamper the messages the page sends?

Yes — match/replace only sees HTTP messages, but a hook can fire on the socket itself. The phase is named after the direction:

```
burpwn --json hook add order-role \
  --phase ws-c2s \
  --action replace-payload \
  --find '"role":"user"' \
  --replace '"role":"admin"' \
  --host app.fintrack.dev
```

```json
{"data": {"hook_id": 1, "name": "order-role"}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

`ws-c2s` is client→server (the messages the page sends); `ws-s2c` is server→client. Those are the words the capture already uses — `req show` prints `c2s`/`s2c` per message — so you can copy what you read. `ws-send`/`ws-client` and `ws-recv`/`ws-server` are accepted as aliases if they come more naturally.

Two things to know about `--find`:

* it is a **literal**, not a regex — `"role":"user"` matches those bytes and nothing else, so no escaping games
* it is binary-safe, so it works on a socket carrying protobuf or MessagePack as well as JSON

The hook fires on one *complete* message, reassembled — not per TCP frame — so a payload split across continuation frames is still matched. An empty `--replace` deletes the matched text. Scope it: without `--host app.fintrack.dev` this would rewrite that string on every socket in the session.

My session tokens on fintrack.dev expire mid-scan and everything starts 401ing. Automate re-auth.

Persist a session-auth profile: the login command, a regex (one capture group) that pulls the token from its output, and the header template to inject:

```
burpwn --json session auth set --login 'curl -s https://auth.fintrack.dev/login -d user=analyst -d pass=s3cr3t' --extract '"token":"([^"]+)"' --header 'Authorization: Bearer {}' --host fintrack.dev
```

Returns {"data": {"hook_id": 1, "host": "fintrack.dev", "id": 1}, "error": null, "ok": true}.

That is already the whole setup — there is no second step to 'activate' it. A profile IS a `pre-request` hook with an `exec` action, stored under the name `auth:fintrack.dev`, and it mints the token **on the request that is waiting**: the first in-scope request parks on the login command, then goes upstream carrying the fresh header. Nobody has to eat a 401 to make the next call work.

`id` and `hook_id` are the same number because they are the same row — `burpwn hook list` shows it alongside your other hooks.
So what does `session auth refresh` do then?

It throws away the token the daemon has **cached**, so the next in-scope request runs the login command again:

```
burpwn --json session auth refresh --host fintrack.dev
```

```json
{"data": {"cleared": [1], "profiles": [{"cleared": true, "hook_id": 1, "host": "fintrack.dev"}]}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

It does **not** run your login command and it does not hand you a token — there is no token in that output because there is no token to report. The value a profile mints is held in the running daemon's memory for the hook's TTL (300000 ms by default) and is written nowhere; `refresh` is a request to that daemon to forget it early.

So you only need it when the token went stale *before* its TTL expired — a server-side logout, a rotated secret. `cleared:[1]` lists the hooks whose cached value was actually dropped; with no daemon running you get `cleared:[]` and `cleared:false` per profile, which is success, not failure: nothing was cached, so the next request already mints.
How do I check what's stored?

```
burpwn --json session auth status
```

```json
{"data": {"profiles": [{"enabled": true, "header_template": "Authorization: Bearer {}", "hook_id": 1, "host": "fintrack.dev", "id": 1, "login_cmd": "curl -s https://auth.fintrack.dev/login -d user=analyst -d pass=s3cr3t", "name": "auth:fintrack.dev", "timeout_ms": 10000, "ttl_ms": 300000}]}, "error": null, "ok": true}
```

What is stored is the *recipe*, not a credential: the login command, the header template, the host scope and the hook's budgets. There is deliberately no `token` field to inspect — asking 'is a token live?' is asking about daemon memory, not about the session file.

`enabled:false` would mean the profile is muted (`burpwn hook disable 1` and `hook enable 1` work on it, because it is just a hook). Re-running `session auth set` for the same host REPLACES this profile rather than stacking a second login command onto every request.

One opsec note: `login_cmd` holds your credentials in plaintext in the session store. `burpwn export session --redact` drops it.
